title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

reading.body:
This is a false positive in an automated identification system that was acted on as though it were a confirmed fact. A license-plate reader misread a single character and returned a match to a stolen vehicle, and that match passed into a police response without an intervening check. The failure sits at the handoff between a screening tool and an enforcement action, which is the point where an unverified alert becomes a person detained at gunpoint.

Catching it would have taken a human comparison of the alert against the plate and the vehicle before detention. Flock's own position is that alerts should be checked independently before enforcement, which places the missing step inside the ordinary use of the product rather than outside it. The sheriff's office attributes the misread to a tinted plate cover and calls the deputy's actions reasonable, so the two accounts describe the same event as a user error and as a product limitation.

What is not established is that the plate cover caused the misread, or that the deputy's actions were reasonable. Those are statements from the parties involved, not findings by an outside body.

reports.title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

summary: Steven Melvin, 42, of York County, South Carolina, was reportedly detained at gunpoint for over five minutes after a Flock Safety license-plate reader misread the first letter of his plate and matched his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle. The sheriff’s office later said an illegal tinted plate cover caused the error and called the deputy’s actions reasonable. Flock said alerts should be checked independently before enforcement.
